1037.title: Luke (18 October)
1037.hook: the physician evangelist, patron of doctors and artists
1037.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Luke on 18 October; doctors, nurses and artists often ask his prayers, and some hospitals and medical guilds bear his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hedwig, the duchess who gave her wealth away to the poor. Your line was the duchess who gave. What did you give from what you had? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

Near the end of the letter to the Colossians, Paul passes on greetings from the people around him. Some get a name and little more. One gets a name and a job: "Luke the most dear physician." That's the man. A companion of Paul, a doctor, someone Paul was glad to have nearby. His name turns up a few times in Paul's letters, always briefly. And yet the Church's tradition puts his name on a whole Gospel and on the Acts of the Apostles. Doctors keep him as their patron. So do painters. Today's word is the evangelist with a doctor's eye.
screen: `A GREETING AT THE END OF A LETTER.` → `LUKE THE MOST DEAR PHYSICIAN.` → `DOCTORS AND PAINTERS CLAIM HIM.`

segments.voice: Start with how his Gospel begins. Before any angel, before any manger, the writer speaks to one person, a man named Theophilus. Others, he says, have set out to tell these things. He has looked into all of it carefully from the start, and now he will write it down in order, so Theophilus can be sure of what he was taught. That's not a poet clearing his throat. That's someone who checks. The Acts of the Apostles opens by speaking to the same Theophilus, which is why tradition reads the two books as one work in two parts, by one hand. Then the doctor's eye. Luke's Gospel is where you meet the good Samaritan bending over a beaten man on the road, pouring in oil and wine and binding up his wounds. It's where the prodigal son comes home hungry and the father runs. It's full of people at the edges: the sick, the poor, widows, outsiders. Some readers hear a physician in that, someone used to sitting with people in their worst week. Now the painters. Tradition says Luke painted Mary, and some old icons of her have been called his. Nobody can prove a brush was ever in his hand. But his first chapters are where Mary stands in full: the angel's greeting, the visit to Elizabeth, the birth, the shepherds. And then one quiet line: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Whether or not he painted her, he gave artists their scenes.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ORDER, FOR THEOPHILUS.` · `ONE WORK IN TWO PARTS.` · `A DOCTOR'S EYE FOR THE WOUNDED.` · `HE GAVE PAINTERS THEIR SCENES.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: draw something. Find a pen and the back of an envelope, a napkin, anything. Choose one thing in front of you, a cup, your own hand, a window. Settle, and breathe. Then draw it slowly, looking at it more than at the page. It doesn't need to be good. The point is to look at one thing long enough to see it, the way a doctor looks at a patient, the way Luke's pages linger on Mary. If you pray, you can offer the looking itself as a prayer. If you don't, just keep your eyes and your hand moving together for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Luke. A companion of Paul, called the most dear physician, whom tradition names as the writer of a Gospel and of Acts, and the patron of doctors and artists.
Your line: the physician. Today, notice one person who is hurting a little, and give them a doctor's kind of attention: unhurried, close, and kind. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

1038.title: Anthony Mary Claret (24 October)
1038.hook: a weaver turned archbishop of Cuba and founder of the Claretians
1038.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Anthony Mary Claret on 24 October, and the Claretian missionaries he founded keep it as their founder's day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke, the companion of Paul who wrote things down in order. Your line was the physician. Who got your unhurried attention? Day one thousand thirty-eight.

A loom is a loud machine. The shuttle flies back and forth, the frame knocks, and a weaver's whole attention lives in the threads, because one slip shows in the cloth for good. In Catalonia, in Spain, a young man grew up in a weaving family and went to work at the looms in Barcelona. He was good at it, good enough that the work filled his head. Years later that same man would be an archbishop on the far side of the ocean, in Cuba, and the founder of a family of missionaries who still carry his name. Today's word is the weaver who kept weaving, just with different thread.
screen: `THE SHUTTLE FLIES.` → `A WEAVER IN BARCELONA.` → `LATER, AN ARCHBISHOP IN CUBA.`

segments.voice: Anthony Mary Claret wrote an account of his own life, and he's honest in it. He says that as a young weaver, even at Mass, his mind was full of looms and patterns, more machinery than prayer. Then, his account says, a line from the Gospel caught him and would not let go: what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul? He left the looms and became a priest. What came next looks like weaving on a larger frame. He walked from town to town in Catalonia preaching, and he wrote small, cheap books and pamphlets so people could take something home. He gathered other priests into a missionary community, the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, known today as the Claretians. Then he was sent to Cuba as archbishop of Santiago. There he kept going on foot and on horseback, visiting parishes, and he spoke against the cruelty done to enslaved people and the poor. That made enemies. His own account tells of a man who attacked him with a knife and wounded him in the face, and of Claret asking that the man be spared. He took as his motto a line of Paul: "For the charity of Christ presseth us." It means the love of Christ pushes, urges, won't let you sit still. A weaver knows that every thread has to be carried all the way across and tied off. Claret seems to have lived that way: start a thing, and see it through.
screen: `HIS MIND FULL OF LOOMS.` · `A LINE FROM THE GOSPEL CAUGHT HIM.` · `PREACHER, WRITER, FOUNDER.` · `ARCHBISHOP IN CUBA, ATTACKED.` · then, large: `THE CHARITY OF CHRIST PRESSETH US.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: finish one task well. Pick something small that's been left half done. A drawer, a reply, a dish in the sink, a form you started. Settle, and breathe once. Then give it two minutes of a weaver's attention: carry the thread all the way across. Do the last little part you usually skip, the wiping down, the final check, the knot at the end. If you pray, you can offer the finished thing to God. If you don't, simply notice what it's like to see one small thing through. The bell holds the time.
Claretians, the missionaries founded by Anthony Mary Claret, a weaver from Catalonia who became a preacher and archbishop of Santiago in Cuba.
Your line: the weaver bishop. Today, when you're tempted to leave something nearly done, carry the thread across and tie it off. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

1039.title: Simon and Jude (28 October)
1039.hook: two little-known apostles; Jude is patron of hopeless cases
1039.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saints Simon and Jude on 28 October, and Catholics pray to Saint Jude for desperate situations, sometimes in a novena.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony Mary Claret, who left the looms to preach. Your line was the weaver bishop. What did you carry all the way across and tie off? Day one thousand thirty-nine.

In Luke's Gospel, Jesus goes up a mountain, prays all night, and in the morning chooses twelve. Then the text simply lists them. Peter and Andrew, James and John, and on down. Near the end come two names that slide past almost unnoticed: "Simon who is called Zelotes," and Jude, the brother of James. Then the list ends with Judas Iscariot, the traitor. Two men chosen in that same morning light, and the Gospels give them barely a line apiece. The Church keeps their feast together. Today's word is the pair.
screen: `A NIGHT OF PRAYER, THEN TWELVE NAMES.` → `TWO NAMES NEAR THE END.` → `BARELY A LINE APIECE.`

segments.voice: Start with Simon. The Gospels tell us almost one thing about him: a nickname. Luke calls him Zelotes, the zealot, and Matthew and Mark call him by another name, the Cananean. What the nickname meant then, readers still discuss. It may mean he was a man of fierce zeal for God and for his people. Some readers think it points to a group that wanted to throw off Roman rule. Either way, Jesus chose a man with fire in him and put him in the same small band as Matthew, a publican who had sat at a tax table. Whatever each thought of the other's past, those two ended up walking the same roads and eating at the same table. Now Jude. In John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, a Judas speaks up, and John is careful to add: not the Iscariot. He asks Jesus why he will show himself to them and not to the whole world. It's a real question, and Jesus answers it with love and a promise of a home. That's nearly all Jude says on the page. Tradition says Simon and Jude later preached far to the east and died as martyrs, which is why they share a feast. Then something odd happened to Jude. His name sounds like the betrayer's, and some say people avoided praying to him for that reason. So, the story goes, he became the saint you turn to last, when everything else has been tried. Catholic devotion calls him the patron of hopeless cases, of lost causes. The forgotten apostle became the one people remember when nobody else is left to ask.
screen: `SIMON, CALLED THE ZEALOT.` · `JUDE, NOT THE ISCARIOT.` · `TRADITION: PREACHERS AND MARTYRS.` · `THE SAINT OF LOST CAUSES.` · then, large: `THE FORGOTTEN APOSTLES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: hold a hopeless case. Settle, and breathe. Let one situation come to mind that seems past fixing. A friendship that went cold. Someone's illness. A problem in the news that never moves. Don't solve it. Just hold it, the way you'd hold something heavy with both hands. If you pray, you can ask Saint Jude to pray for it, as some Catholics do. If you don't, simply keep it in mind with care for two minutes, and let it be seen instead of filed away. The bell holds the time.
Zelotes, Luke's name for Simon the zealot. He and Jude, not the Iscariot, are two of the twelve whom tradition calls martyrs and whose feast the Church keeps together.
Your line: the forgotten apostles. Today, notice someone in the background of a room, the one who rarely gets named, and say their name kindly. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Josaphat (12 November)
1040.hook: a Ukrainian Greek Catholic archbishop killed in the struggles over unity
1040.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Josaphat on 12 November; Ukrainian Greek Catholics and other Eastern Catholics honor him with particular devotion, and Catholics often pray for Christian unity on his feast.

segments.voice: Last time, Simon and Jude, two apostles the Gospels barely mention. Your line was the forgotten apostles. Whose name did you say kindly? Day one thousand forty.

On the night before he dies, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays out loud for his friends. Then he widens the prayer to people who will believe later, people he will never meet in the flesh. And he asks one thing for all of them: "That they all may be one." Christians have carried that line for a long time, and they have not always kept it. Sometimes the arguments over what unity means have been fierce. Today's saint lived inside one of those arguments, and it cost him his life. Today's word is a monk from the lands of Ukraine and Belarus who became an archbishop.
screen: `A PRAYER ON THE LAST NIGHT.` → `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` → `A LINE NOT ALWAYS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Josaphat grew up in the Eastern Christian world, the world of icons, of the Byzantine liturgy sung in Church Slavonic, of married parish priests and long fasts. In his time some bishops of that church entered into union with the bishop of Rome. They kept their own liturgy, their own customs, their own way of praying, and they accepted the pope's authority. Others refused, and stayed with the Orthodox Church. Families, towns and parishes were split. Josaphat became a monk, then archbishop of Polotsk, on the side of the union. He preached, he cared for the poor, and he worked hard to bring people into the union he believed in. Here's the honest part. The struggle was bitter, and historians record harsh pressure and anger on more than one side. Josaphat was killed by a crowd in a town of his diocese, by people opposed to the union. The Catholic Church honors him as a martyr. Orthodox Christians remember those same years with their own wounds, and the two churches still tell that history differently. That's why his feast can be a hard one, and why the practice today isn't about winning. Today Catholic and Orthodox Christians meet, talk and sometimes pray together. The Eastern Catholic churches, like the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church that especially honors Josaphat, hold together two things: an Eastern way of worship and communion with Rome. His life asks what unity costs, and who pays it.
screen: `AN EASTERN CHRISTIAN WORLD.` · `UNION WITH ROME, AND A SPLIT.` · `KILLED IN THE STRUGGLE.` · `REMEMBERED DIFFERENTLY BY TWO CHURCHES.` · then, large: `DIED FOR UNITY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: hold Christian unity in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind Christians who are not like each other: a Catholic parish, an Orthodox church with its icons, a Protestant congregation down the road. Pick the one you know least, and name one thing its people love: a hymn, a fast, a way of reading the Bible, a saint. Let that one thing stand on its own, with no comparison. If you pray, you can pray the line from John's Gospel, that they all may be one. If you don't, simply wish that community well for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Josaphat. An Eastern Catholic monk and archbishop of Polotsk, killed in the struggle over union with Rome, and honored by the Catholic Church as a martyr.
Your line: died for unity. Today, in one disagreement, look for the thing you and the other person share before you speak. Day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Albert the Great (15 November)
1041.hook: teacher of Aquinas and a scientist of plants and stars, patron of scientists
1041.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Albert the Great on 15 November; Catholic scientists and schools of science sometimes take him as patron and mark his feast with a Mass.

segments.voice: Last time, Josaphat, the archbishop killed in the struggle over union with Rome. Your line was died for unity. Where did you look for common ground? Day one thousand forty-one.

A leaf, held up to the light. The veins branch like rivers. The edge is toothed or smooth. One side is darker than the other. A medieval friar spent hours looking at things like this, and at birds, stones, insects and the night sky, and then he wrote it all down. He also taught theology, ran a house of studies, served as a bishop, and had among his students a large, quiet young man named Thomas Aquinas. The Church calls him a Doctor of the Church, and the patron of people who study the natural world. Today's word is the friar with the leaf in his hand.
screen: `A LEAF HELD TO THE LIGHT.` → `BIRDS, STONES, STARS.` → `AND A STUDENT NAMED THOMAS.`

segments.voice: Albert was a German Dominican friar, a preacher and teacher, and people came to call him the Great. He read everything he could find, including the old Greek philosopher Aristotle, whom some Christians of his day found suspect. Albert didn't. He thought the whole world was God's work, so honest study of it could only lead toward God, never away. And he did more than read. He wrote about plants and animals and minerals, and he said, in effect, that in these matters you have to check for yourself, by looking and testing, and not just repeat what the books say. Some of his notes are his own observations. That's the friar with the leaf. Then the student. Tradition tells that Thomas Aquinas was so big and so silent that his classmates called him the dumb ox. Albert, the story goes, told them that one day this ox would bellow so loud the whole world would hear. Thomas went on to become one of the great teachers of the Church, and Albert had seen it coming. There's an old thread in the Bible that runs under his life. In the book of Job, Job tells his friends to ask the animals and the birds, and the earth itself, and they will teach. Albert's work reads like someone taking that line at its word: if the world is God's work, then a plant is a kind of page. That's why the Church names him patron of those who study the natural world.
screen: `A FRIAR WHO READ EVERYTHING.` · `CHECK FOR YOURSELF.` · `THE TEACHER OF THOMAS.` · `ASK THE BEASTS; THEY WILL TEACH.` · then, large: `A PLANT IS A PAGE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: learn one plant. Find one, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a tree outside the window, or even a picture of one. Settle, and breathe. Then look the way Albert looked. The shape of the leaves. How they attach to the stem. The color on each side. Where it's growing and what it seems to need. If you like, find out its name afterward. If you pray, you can thank God for it, plainly. If you don't, simply let it hold your full attention for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Albert. A German Dominican friar, teacher of Thomas Aquinas, a writer on plants, animals and stars, a Doctor of the Church and patron of scientists.
Your line: patron of science. Today, when you hear a claim about the natural world, do what Albert did: go and look for yourself. Day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Margaret of Scotland (16 November)
1042.hook: a queen who fed orphans and the poor before she ate
1042.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Margaret of Scotland on 16 November; in Scotland she is honored as a patron, and a small chapel in Edinburgh Castle bears her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Albert, the friar with a leaf in his hand. Your line was patron of science. What plant did you get to know? Day one thousand forty-two.

The man who heard her confessions wrote her life after she died, and he kept one morning scene in it. Before the queen of Scotland eats a thing, small children with no parents are brought in. She takes them on her knee, she feeds them herself, sometimes with her own spoon, and only after that does she sit down to her own meal. A queen, with servants for everything, choosing to do this part with her own hands. Today's word is the queen who ate second.
screen: `MORNING IN A ROYAL HOUSE.` → `THE CHILDREN EAT FIRST.` → `THE QUEEN EATS SECOND.`

segments.voice: Margaret was born a princess of the old English royal family, in exile, far from England. The usual account says that after the Norman conquest her family fled, and their ship came to Scotland, where she married King Malcolm. Her confessor, a monk named Turgot, wrote her life, and most of what's told here comes from it. He describes a woman of long prayers and hard fasting who still kept a busy court and raised a large family. And he describes the poor, everywhere around her. She fed orphans before she ate. She served the poor at table herself, sometimes with the king beside her. She gave away so much that, Turgot says, the king's own treasure was raided for alms, and Malcolm pretended not to notice. One small detail has stayed with readers. Malcolm, Turgot says, could not read. But he saw how his wife loved her books, so he would pick them up and kiss them, and he had some of them covered in gold and jewels for her. A king who could not read, honoring what his wife loved. Behind all of this stands a line from Matthew's Gospel, where the King at the end says to those on his right: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." They ask when, and he answers that whatever they did for the least of his brethren, they did for him. Margaret seems to have heard that literally. If Christ was in the hungry child, then the hungry child was fed before the queen. That's the order her life keeps: first the poor.
screen: `A PRINCESS IN EXILE.` · `HER CONFESSOR WROTE HER LIFE.` · `THE KING WHO KISSED HER BOOKS.` · `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.` · then, large: `FIRST THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: feed someone before yourself. It can be very small. At your next meal, serve someone else first, or set aside a share for someone who needs it, or put food in a donation bin before you buy your own. For now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the person, or the place, you'll feed first today. Imagine handing it over, and only then turning to your own plate. If you pray, you can ask Margaret's help to see Christ in the one you feed. If you don't, simply hold that person in mind with care for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Margaret. A queen, wife of King Malcolm, who fed orphans and served the poor before she ate, as her confessor Turgot remembered her.
Your line: first the poor. Today, before you take your own share of something, food or time or attention, give someone else theirs. Day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: Gertrude the Great (16 November)
1043.hook: a German nun whose visions centered on the heart of Christ
1043.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Gertrude on 16 November; Benedictine and Cistercian communities read from her writings, and some Catholics pray her prayers as part of devotion to the Sacred Heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Margaret, the queen who fed orphans before she ate. Your line was first the poor. Who got their share before you? Day one thousand forty-three.

At the Last Supper, John's Gospel gives a small, close detail: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." A head resting on a chest. Close enough to hear a heartbeat. The Gospel says nothing more about it. Long afterward, a nun in a German monastery wondered about exactly that. If the beloved disciple was that close, why didn't he write down what he heard? Today's word is the nun who asked, and the answer she wrote.
screen: `A HEAD ON JESUS'S CHEST.` → `CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR A HEARTBEAT.` → `A NUN ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Gertrude lived in the monastery of Helfta, in Germany, a house of women known for learning. She came there as a child and grew up among books. She loved study, Latin, the classics, and by her own account she loved them a little too much. Then, she writes, Christ came to her in a vision, gently, and she turned from being a scholar who happened to pray to someone whose whole life was prayer. She wrote down what she received in a book usually called The Herald of Divine Love, and some of it was written by her sisters from what she told them. At the center of it is the heart of Christ. Not as a symbol on a card, but as a place: a home she could rest in, a fire, a fountain. In one of her visions, on the feast of John, she rests near the beloved disciple and asks him the question from the hook. You leaned on that chest. You heard that heart. Why did you write nothing about it? And John, in her vision, answers that his task was to speak of the Word, for the early Church. The sweetness of those heartbeats, he says, was saved for a later time, when the world had grown cold and needed warming. Some readers see in Gertrude an early voice of the devotion that Catholics later called the Sacred Heart. Whatever the history, her point is simple. For her, God's love isn't only an idea. It has a pulse. Heart, in her writing, means the place where God's love and a person's love meet.

segments.voice: Today's practice: pray from the heart, or simply listen to it. Settle, and breathe. Rest a hand on your chest and find your own heartbeat. Let it set the pace for a while. No words needed. If you pray, you can rest there the way Gertrude pictured John resting, and let any words come slowly, or not at all. If you don't, just stay with the beat under your hand for two minutes, and notice the life that's been keeping time for you all along. The bell holds the time.
Gertrude. A nun of Helfta in Germany whose visions, written in The Herald of Divine Love, center on the heart of Christ.

Your line: the heart. That closes a week of saints: Luke the physician, Claret the weaver, Simon and Jude, Josaphat, Albert, Margaret, and now Gertrude. Today, once, put your hand over your heart and pause before you answer someone. Day one thousand forty-three.
